text: THE DEVIL BIRD.

label: text
text: BAFFLING MYSTERY OF CEVLON

label: text
text: CHE PLANTER'S STORY.

label: text
text: The following are extracts from a paper read by Dr. Spittel at a meeting of the Coylon Natural History Society:

label: text
text: Always fascinating and alluring is the unknown. " The Devil Bird is on the many mysteries of our Island. Like the Singing Fish of the " Batticalou lagoon, it has continued to battle us. Long may they both continue to do so.

label: text
text: The Devil, Bird owes its nume not to its appearance which, if I know it, is lundsome; but to its voice, which is eerie and appalling, and leened only in wild places in the silence of night.

label: text
text: The human mind has a leaning to the supernatural; and one may pardon the extravagantly fanciful descriptions that have characterised the reports of most of those who have had the good fortune to hear this bird. Here, for instance, is the story as told by an old-time plunter.

label: text
text: "It was just before the breaking of the big monsoon. "The night was warm and close. I had been dining at a friend's and was riding home quietly and soberly along the bridle-path, in and out among the deep ravines. Suddenly there was a cry; then another still more piercing, and my pony, a brisk, black, little Pegu, corked his ears and bolted. He flew, and in the twist of a rivine he had me off like a shot. There I'lav on my back, kicking and struggling and crying blue murder. And all the time shriek followed shriek, curdling my very marrow; and the mountains shrieked in concertly until my cheek pulled and I began to pray.

label: paragraph_title
text: ATTRIBUTED TO OWL8.

label: text
text: "At last they died away—those awful cries—in one long inearthly wait, I rolled out more dead than alive, got home and went to bed. I did not then know there was such a thing as a devil-bird in the Island. I certainly thought some wretched girl was being killed. I never slept a wink, but got up before the sun, and went down to the next village to rout the villains out, and there got to know all about it. " "You see," said the headman, "lift night one of our women died in labour, and her spirit went at once into a devil-bird, which must have been sitting handy. So when your Majesty hears a devil-bird again, lie still, for it is always the soul of a woman in panga, and it's best to give it a wide berth."

label: text
text: What then is the Devil Bird? So far, the consensus of recorded opinion seems to be that it is an Owl—the Brown Wood Owl ("strix indrancee"), Tennant, Layard, Kelaart, Legge, Neville and many others accepted this view; and today if you ask at our museum to be shown the Devil Bird, starix indrancee will be the bird pointed out to you.

label: text
text: Tegge is very unconvincing in his attempts at proving the bird's identity; and Neville seems to be tied up rather in knots, seriously giving as possible solutions of the cry. "The dreadful shrieks, like those of a young child, or those made by frogs in the jaws of rat-makes or in the cruel talons of a night hawk."

label: paragraph_title
text: GRIM SEUGGESTIVENESS.

label: text
text: It is the human note in these series that is their appalling feature; the one that of a lost soul, the other that of a person being garotted. What wonder the villagers in the localities the bird accustomed to hunt, hold it in holy terror, and its cry as of ill omen. So much so that if it be heard when a person is seriously ill, his relations will not bother much about him, but leave him to his fate, saying intervention is useless. They will run away from the sound, if it be heard close and stay hushed indoors.

label: text
text: There are scores of people in Ceylon who have shot the Devil Bird while it cried: only they are not the people who write about such things. I myself know half a dozen of them and the descriptions of every one were in agreement.

label: text
text: Only four days ago I asked a man who had spent a great part of his life in the forests whether he knew what the Devil Bird was like.

label: text
text: "It is an Engle with a crested head," he promptly replied.

label: text
text: "How do you know?" I asked. "I shot one while it was "hooting" and ogling on a large dead tree one moonlight night by my camp," he said. "I not only shot it, but ate its flesh to prov to my terror-stricken coolies, who ran away when they first heard the cry, that it was no demion but a bird." That is the kind of evidence I have repeatedly elicited from reliable informants.

label: text
text: Now the question is: Are the two cries—the long drawn hoo-oo, and the guttural chortle, so unitative of a person being strangled—made by the same bird or by different species?

label: text
text: The cry of the Devil Bird is generally heard early in the night, at midnight, and towards dawn. The boo cry can be heard far the

label: paragraph_title
text: LOCAL STRIKE.

label: text
text: SHANGHAI PAPER'S COMMENT.

label: text
text: in some respects, are really separate and apart, remarks "Shipping and Engineering" (Shanghai). While the peg on which the excuse for the Shanghai strike was hung was the Nanking Road shooting affair, there has been no such excuse for the walk-out at Hongkong, and the affair has been from the beginning; an openly anti-British movement, engineered and financed by the Bolshevist element which is so powerful in the Province of Kwangtung, and in Canton particularly. With the foreigners in China—and the British and Japanese particularly—already experiencing great trouble in regard to the Shanghai strike and the general stoppage of shipping, the Bolshevists at Canton were not slow in utilising the opportunity of striking another blow at Great Britain through, the medium of the great port of Hongkong. It will be remembered that on June 12 the Yunnanese troops who had been in charge of Canton for so long were overwhelmingly routed by the Bolshevist forces, under the wing and guidance of Soviet emissaries, and that as a result of that victory a horrible revolting massacre of the defeated Yunnanese took place in Canton. It is well known that the Seamen's Union (of Chinese) which has a branch in Shanghai has its headquarters at Canton, and that the leaders of that Union are frankly and avowedly Bolshevist-inclined. It is perhaps hardly to be wondered at, therefore, that when the Bolsheviks assumed full and unfittered control of the Kwangtung capital they should take the first opportunity of adding to the trouble in those parts by engineering a general strike of all kinds of workers in Hongkong. The machinery for such a move was, apparently, all ready, and the strike commenced to take serious effect in Hongkong on June 19/20, and quickly embraced all of the essential and non-essential services affecting the Colony, including the most important of all, shipping. In a short few days the commerce of the port was practically tied up; all manner of Chinese employees, from workers in Government departments to houseboys, dockyard workers and seamen walked out, or, rather, went out under the duress of intimidation; and at the end of the month Hongkong, as Shanghai, was carrying on as best it could—and a very good best, be it understood—with foreigners (including Americans and other nationalities), doing their utmost and taking part in all manner of services, protectional, governmental and commercial, in order to keep things going. And so the situation is at the end of June: Strikers in all departments of activity in the Colony, trade disorganised and every foreigner doing his best to help to carry on. The Hongkong strike is wholly one where the forces of intimidation have been supreme. It is certain that not one per cent. of the men out have wanted to go on strike, or that they have any serious grievance against their employers, or the Hongkong Government, or the British people generally. It is simply a move in the gigantic Bolshevist scheme to get China under domination, to ruin foreign trade with the country and to abrogate foreign influence.
